title: Physio Mistakes to Avoid With Arthritis: 15 Common Pitfalls and What to Do Instead

content:
Quick answer: The most common physio mistakes with arthritis are not doing home exercises regularly, doing them too fast or too hard, stopping when pain flares instead of adjusting, never progressing, expecting quick results, and stopping once appointments end. To get the most from physiotherapy, prepare questions, agree clear goals, follow a written plan and keep exercising long term.

Physiotherapy is one of the most effective ways to manage arthritis. NICE guideline NG226 recommends exercise tailored to the person as a core treatment for osteoarthritis, and physiotherapists are experts in setting it up. But physiotherapy is not something that is done to you: most of the benefit comes from what you do between and after appointments. Many people get less from physio than they could, often because of a few common, fixable mistakes. This guide explains 15 of them and what to do instead, so you can make the most of every appointment.

Before your appointments

Mistake 1: Waiting too long to ask for help

Many people put up with pain and stiffness for months or years before seeing a physiotherapist, by which time muscles have weakened and habits are harder to change. Instead: ask for help early. In many parts of the UK you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy without seeing a GP first. Our guide to self-referral versus GP referral explains how. If there is a wait, start gentle exercise in the meantime; our guide to NHS physio waiting lists suggests what to do.

Mistake 2: Turning up unprepared

Appointments are often short, and it is easy to forget important details. Instead: before your first appointment, write down:

  • which joints are affected and how long you have had symptoms
  • what makes your pain better or worse
  • what you are struggling to do, such as stairs, walking to the shops, gardening or work tasks
  • your medicines and other health conditions
  • what you have already tried
  • your questions

Wear loose clothing so the physio can see and move the affected joints, such as shorts for knee problems.

Mistake 3: Not saying what matters to you

A plan that does not connect to your life is harder to stick to. Instead: tell your physio your goals in everyday terms, such as "walk my dog for 30 minutes", "get up from the floor when playing with my grandchildren" or "manage a full shift at work". Good physiotherapy is built around these goals.

During your appointments

Mistake 4: Expecting a passive treatment to fix things

Massage, manual therapy, heat and other hands-on treatments may help some people feel more comfortable in the short term, but NICE advises that they should only be used alongside exercise, not on their own. Instead: see exercise as the main treatment, and hands-on treatments, if used, as extras that make exercise easier.

Mistake 5: Not understanding your exercises before you leave

It is common to leave an appointment and realise at home that you are not sure how to do an exercise. Instead: ask to practise each exercise while your physio watches, and ask for a written or online exercise sheet with pictures. Some people find it helpful to take a photo or short video, if the physio agrees. Make sure you know how many repetitions, how often, and what to do if it hurts.

Mistake 6: Not mentioning worries or other symptoms

Fear of making things worse is one of the biggest barriers to exercise with arthritis. Instead: tell your physio what you are worried about. They can explain what is safe, what pain is normal and what is a warning sign. Also mention any new symptoms, such as swelling in other joints, numbness, unexplained weight loss or feeling generally unwell.

With your home exercises

Mistake 7: Not doing them regularly

Home exercises are the core of physiotherapy, and benefits come from regular practice over weeks and months. Instead: build them into your routine, for example after breakfast or while the kettle boils. Use a simple tick chart on the fridge or a phone reminder. If the plan is too long to fit into your day, ask for a shorter version; doing a short plan consistently is better than an ideal plan you cannot keep up.

Mistake 8: Rushing the movements

Fast, jerky repetitions use momentum rather than muscle and may irritate joints. Instead: move slowly and with control, taking around 2 to 3 seconds to lift and 2 to 3 seconds to lower, and breathe normally.

Mistake 9: Doing too much too soon

On a good day it is tempting to double your exercises or add new ones, which can lead to a flare. Instead: stick to the plan and increase gradually, one change at a time. Our exercise progression guide has a simple decision table for when to step up, hold or step back.

Mistake 10: Stopping completely when it hurts

Some discomfort during exercise is normal with arthritis and does not mean you are causing damage. Stopping completely often leads to more stiffness and weakness. Instead: use a pain guide. Many physiotherapists suggest that pain during exercise should stay at a level you find acceptable (often around 4 out of 10 or lower) and settle within 24 hours. If it does not, reduce the repetitions, range or resistance, rather than stopping. During a flare, switch to gentler movement; see our guide to exercise during a flare-up.

Mistake 11: Ignoring sharp or worrying pain

The opposite mistake is pushing through pain that is a warning sign. Instead: stop an exercise if you get sharp, stabbing pain, a joint locking or giving way, or significant new swelling, and contact your physio for advice.

Mistake 12: Never progressing

Doing the same easy exercises for months keeps you ticking over, but muscles only get stronger when they are gradually challenged. Instead: when an exercise feels easy and your joints are fine, increase repetitions, sets or resistance, or ask your physio for the next level.

Mistake 13: Only doing the exercises, and not being active

Home exercises are important, but they are not the whole picture. Instead: combine them with general activity such as walking, cycling or swimming, building towards the UK guideline of 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, if you can. NICE recommends both muscle strengthening and aerobic exercise.

After physiotherapy ends

Mistake 14: Expecting quick results and giving up

Strength builds over weeks to months. Many people expect to feel better after one or two sessions and give up when they do not. Instead: give it time. Many people notice everyday tasks getting easier after a few weeks, with clearer strength gains after 8 to 12 weeks. Track small wins, such as fewer rests on a walk or easier stairs.

Mistake 15: Stopping once appointments end

NHS physiotherapy is usually a short course, but arthritis is long term. The benefits of exercise fade if you stop. Instead: before your last appointment, ask for a long-term plan: which exercises to keep doing, how often, how to progress, and what to do if you have a flare. Consider a local class, gym or exercise referral scheme to keep you going, and know how to get back in touch if things change.

Common mistakes by joint

JointCommon mistakeTry instead
KneeAvoiding all bending and stairs, so thigh muscles weakenStrengthen thighs with sit-to-stands and step-ups, within comfort
HipOnly stretching and never strengthening the buttock musclesAdd bridges, side leg raises and sit-to-stands
HandSqueezing stress balls hard and often during a flareGentle range-of-motion first; add grip work only when settled
ShoulderForcing the arm overhead through painWork in a comfortable range and strengthen the rotator cuff with light resistance
BackResting in bed for long periodsKeep moving with short walks and gentle exercises
Foot and ankleExercising in unsupportive footwearWear supportive, cushioned shoes for standing exercises

Mistakes with pain relief and other treatments

  • Relying on pain relief instead of exercise. Medicines can make exercise easier, but NICE recommends exercise as the core treatment for osteoarthritis.
  • Not timing pain relief. If your doctor or pharmacist has advised pain relief, taking it at a suitable time before exercise may help. Check with them first.
  • Using a support or brace all day. Supports can help for specific tasks, but wearing them constantly can lead to weaker muscles unless advised by your clinician.
  • Stopping other treatments. If you have inflammatory arthritis, keep taking your prescribed medicines; physio works alongside them.

What a good physio plan looks like

A good plan is personal, realistic and clear. It should include agreed goals, a short list of exercises with written instructions, how many and how often, how hard it should feel, a pain guide, how to progress, what to do during a flare, and how to keep going after discharge. If any of these are missing, it is fine to ask.

Quick self-check

QuestionIf the answer is no
Do I know my goals and what my plan is for?Ask your physio to agree goals with you
Do I have a written or online copy of my exercises?Ask for one at your next appointment
Am I doing my exercises most days, as advised?Shorten the plan or link it to a daily habit
Do I know what level of pain is acceptable?Ask your physio to explain the pain guide
Have I progressed my exercises in the last month?Use the decision table or ask for the next level
Am I doing general activity as well?Add short walks or another low-impact activity
Do I know what to do when physio ends?Ask for a long-term plan before discharge

Questions to ask your physiotherapist

  • What do you think is causing my symptoms?
  • Which exercises are most important if I am short of time?
  • How much pain is acceptable during and after exercise?
  • How and when should I make my exercises harder?
  • What should I do if I have a flare?
  • Are there activities I should avoid, or ones you would encourage?
  • Would splints, insoles, a walking aid or an occupational therapy referral help me?
  • How do I get back in touch after discharge?

Getting the most from different types of physio

TypeTips
Face-to-face, one-to-onePrepare questions, practise exercises during the session
Telephone or videoFind a quiet space with room to move; have a chair and your exercise sheet ready
Group classes or exercise programmesTell the instructor about your joints; work at your own level; the social side can help motivation
Apps and online programmesCheck that they are recommended by your physio or the NHS; report any problems
Private physiotherapyCheck that the physio is registered with the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC); ask about costs and expected number of sessions

When to go back to your physio or GP

  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature.
  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness, or signs of a stroke.
  • Contact your physio if exercises consistently make pain worse for more than 24 hours, if a joint locks or gives way, or if you are not improving after 6 to 8 weeks of doing your exercises regularly.
  • See your GP if you have new swelling in several joints, long morning stiffness, unexplained weight loss, fever, or numbness or weakness in a limb.

To learn more about how physiotherapy helps, see our guide to physiotherapy for arthritis.

How often should I do my physio exercises?

Follow your physiotherapist's advice. Many strengthening programmes are done 2 to 3 times a week, and mobility exercises daily. Doing them consistently matters more than doing a lot at once.

Is it normal for physio exercises to hurt?

Some discomfort is normal with arthritis. Pain should stay at a level you find acceptable and settle within 24 hours. Sharp pain, locking or new swelling are reasons to stop and get advice.

What if my physio exercises are not working?

Check whether you are doing them regularly, slowly and with gradual progression. If you are, and you have not improved after 6 to 8 weeks, contact your physio to review your plan.

How long does physiotherapy take to work for arthritis?

Many people notice some improvement within a few weeks, but strength and function usually continue to improve over 3 months or more of regular exercise.

Can I see a physio without a GP referral?

In many areas of the UK, yes. Check your local NHS service or GP practice website for self-referral options.

Should I carry on with exercises after physio ends?

Yes. Arthritis is long term, and exercise benefits fade if you stop. Ask your physio for a long-term plan before your last appointment.
